claim: Up-regulation of the persistent sodium current (INaP) leads to spasticity after spinal cord injury (SCI).
source: Up-regulation of the persistent sodium current (INaP) and down-regulation of the potassium/chloride extruder KCC2 lead to spasticity after spinal cord injury (SCI).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is part of the established scientific context for the study.

claim: Down-regulation of the potassium/chloride extruder KCC2 leads to spasticity after spinal cord injury (SCI).
source: Up-regulation of the persistent sodium current (INaP) and down-regulation of the potassium/chloride extruder KCC2 lead to spasticity after spinal cord injury (SCI).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is part of the established scientific context for the study.

claim: Calpain is the driver of the up-regulation of INaP in neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons after SCI.
source: We here identified calpain as the driver of the up- and down-regulation of INaP and KCC2, respectively, in neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Calpain is the driver of the down-regulation of KCC2 in neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons after SCI.
source: We here identified calpain as the driver of the up- and down-regulation of INaP and KCC2, respectively, in neonatal rat lumbar motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Few days after SCI, neonatal rats developed behavioral signs of spasticity with the emergence of hyperreflexia.
source: Few days after SCI, neonatal rats developed behavioral signs of spasticity with the emergence of both hyperreflexia and abnormal involuntary muscle contractions on hindlimbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Few days after SCI, neonatal rats developed behavioral signs of spasticity with the emergence of abnormal involuntary muscle contractions on hindlimbs.
source: Few days after SCI, neonatal rats developed behavioral signs of spasticity with the emergence of both hyperreflexia and abnormal involuntary muscle contractions on hindlimbs.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: In vitro isolated lumbar spinal cords became hyperreflexive after SCI.
source: At the same time, in vitro isolated lumbar spinal cords became hyperreflexive and displayed numerous spontaneous motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: In vitro isolated lumbar spinal cords displayed numerous spontaneous motor outputs after SCI.
source: At the same time, in vitro isolated lumbar spinal cords became hyperreflexive and displayed numerous spontaneous motor outputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Calpain-I expression paralleled with a proteolysis of voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels after SCI.
source: Calpain-I expression paralleled with a proteolysis of voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels and KCC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Calpain-I expression paralleled with a proteolysis of KCC2 after SCI.
source: Calpain-I expression paralleled with a proteolysis of voltage-gated sodium (Nav) channels and KCC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced the proteolysis of Nav channels and KCC2.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using MDL28170 presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains restored the motoneuronal expression of KCC2.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains normalized INaP function.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains normalized KCC2 function.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings of EIPSP presented in Figure 4.

claim: Acute inhibition of calpains curtailed spasticity.
source: Acute inhibition of calpains reduced this proteolysis, restored the motoneuronal expression of Nav and KCC2, normalized INaP and KCC2 function, and curtailed spasticity.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav drives the hyperexcitability of motoneurons which leads to spasticity after SCI.
source: In sum, by up- and down-regulating INaP and KCC2, the calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav and KCC2 drives the hyperexcitability of motoneurons which leads to spasticity after SCI.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined experimental data from the study.

claim: The calpain-mediated proteolysis of KCC2 drives the hyperexcitability of motoneurons which leads to spasticity after SCI.
source: In sum, by up- and down-regulating INaP and KCC2, the calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav and KCC2 drives the hyperexcitability of motoneurons which leads to spasticity after SCI.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the combined experimental data from the study.

claim: Hyperexcitability of motoneurons develops after spinal cord injury due in part to the hyperexcitability of motoneurons.
source: The main clinical symptoms of spasticity, hyperreflexia and spasms, develop after spinal cord injury (SCI) due in part to the hyperexcitability of motoneurons (Hultborn, 2003; Gorassini, 2004; Nielsen et al., 2007; D'Amico et al., 2014; Thomas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their persistent sodium (INaP) currents.
source: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their persistent sodium (INaP) and calcium (ICaP) currents, leading to muscle spasms and hyperreflexia in both humans and adult rats (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Harvey et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2006b; Harvey et al., 2006a; ElBasiouny et al., 2010; Theiss et al., 2011; Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their calcium (ICaP) currents.
source: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their persistent sodium (INaP) and calcium (ICaP) currents, leading to muscle spasms and hyperreflexia in both humans and adult rats (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Harvey et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2006b; Harvey et al., 2006a; ElBasiouny et al., 2010; Theiss et al., 2011; Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Upregulation of persistent inward currents leads to muscle spasms in humans and adult rats.
source: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their persistent sodium (INaP) and calcium (ICaP) currents, leading to muscle spasms and hyperreflexia in both humans and adult rats (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Harvey et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2006b; Harvey et al., 2006a; ElBasiouny et al., 2010; Theiss et al., 2011; Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Upregulation of persistent inward currents leads to hyperreflexia in humans and adult rats.
source: SCI enhances the intrinsic excitability of motoneurons by upregulating their persistent sodium (INaP) and calcium (ICaP) currents, leading to muscle spasms and hyperreflexia in both humans and adult rats (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Harvey et al., 2005; Harvey et al., 2006b; Harvey et al., 2006a; ElBasiouny et al., 2010; Theiss et al., 2011; Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: A concomitant synaptic disinhibition of motoneurons due to a decrease of the main chloride extruder KCC2 takes place after SCI in both humans and adult rodents.
source: In addition, a concomitant synaptic disinhibition of motoneurons due to a decrease of the main chloride extruder KCC2 also takes place after SCI in both humans and adult rodents (Boulenguez et al., 2010; Mòdol et al., 2014; Klomjai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Disinhibition after SCI stems primarily from an impaired Cl− extrusion in neonatal rats.
source: In vitro experiments from neonatal rats show that this form of disinhibition stems primarily from an impaired Cl− extrusion, typically identified by a depolarizing shift of the reversal potential of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (EIPSP) (Boulenguez et al., 2010), which may facilitate the recruitment of persistent inward currents after SCI (Venugopal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Impaired Cl− extrusion is typically identified by a depolarizing shift of the reversal potential of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (EIPSP).
source: In vitro experiments from neonatal rats show that this form of disinhibition stems primarily from an impaired Cl− extrusion, typically identified by a depolarizing shift of the reversal potential of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (EIPSP) (Boulenguez et al., 2010), which may facilitate the recruitment of persistent inward currents after SCI (Venugopal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Impaired Cl− extrusion may facilitate the recruitment of persistent inward currents after SCI.
source: In vitro experiments from neonatal rats show that this form of disinhibition stems primarily from an impaired Cl− extrusion, typically identified by a depolarizing shift of the reversal potential of inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (EIPSP) (Boulenguez et al., 2010), which may facilitate the recruitment of persistent inward currents after SCI (Venugopal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and involves speculative reasoning about mechanisms.

claim: Up-regulation of persistent inward currents concomitant with down-regulation of KCC2 may have a synergistic effect causing spasticity.
source: Thus, up-regulation of persistent inward currents concomitant with down-regulation of KCC2 may have a synergistic effect causing spasticity.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the combined effects described in the literature.

claim: SCI-induced constitutive 5-HT2B/C receptor activity leads to an increase in ICaP.
source: SCI-induced constitutive 5-HT2B/C receptor activity leads to an increase in ICaP (Murray et al., 2010), while calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav1.6 channels up-regulates INaP (Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav1.6 channels up-regulates INaP.
source: SCI-induced constitutive 5-HT2B/C receptor activity leads to an increase in ICaP (Murray et al., 2010), while calpain-mediated proteolysis of Nav1.6 channels up-regulates INaP (Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calpain-mediated cleavage of KCC2 depolarizes the EIPSP in some pathophysiological conditions.
source: Although the mechanisms involved in alterations of KCC2 after SCI remain elusive, it is worth mentioning that calpain-mediated cleavage of KCC2 depolarizes the EIPSP in some pathophysiological conditions (Puskarjov et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2012; Wan et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rats with SCI displayed hindlimb hyperextension characterized by long-lasting EMG activity recorded from triceps surae extensor muscles.
source: Instead of a brief kicking of hindlimbs in response to the tail-pinch test (Figure 1A and Figure 1—video 1), rats with SCI displayed hindlimb hyperextension characterized by long-lasting EMG activity recorded from triceps surae extensor muscles (p<0.001; Figure 1A–C and Figure 1—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data presented in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The threshold for response to mechanical stimuli was significantly reduced in rats with SCI.
source: In addition, the threshold for response to mechanical stimuli was significantly reduced (p<0.05; Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Rats with SCI showed a higher number of spontaneous muscle twitches from the tail and hindlimbs compared to sham-operated rats.
source: Rats with SCI resting on a heated plate at 34°C (Figure 1E) showed a higher number of spontaneous muscle twitches from the tail and hindlimbs compared to sham-operated rats (p<0.001; Figure 1F and Figure 1—videos 3–4).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1E-F.

claim: Behavioral indicators of spasticity emerge a few days after SCI in neonatal rats.
source: In sum, behavioral indicators of spasticity emerge a few days after SCI in neonatal rats.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Bath-applied MDL28170 (30 µM, 60 min) reduced dorsal root-evoked ventral root responses.
source: Bath-applied MDL28170 (30 µM, 60 min) reduced dorsal root-evoked ventral root responses (Figure 4A) to the point that the PSTH approximated a unimodal distribution (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4A-B.

claim: MDL28170 reduced both SLR and LLR.
source: Both SLR and LLR decreased (p<0.05; Figure 4C) without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p>0.05; insets in Figure 4A and histograms in Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: MDL28170 did not affect the monosynaptic reflex.
source: Both SLR and LLR decreased (p<0.05; Figure 4C) without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p>0.05; insets in Figure 4A and histograms in Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4C.

claim: Spontaneous bursting activity became scarce, shorter and smaller in the presence of MDL28170.
source: Likewise, spontaneous bursting activity became scarce, shorter and smaller in the presence of MDL28170 (p<0.05; Figure 4D–E) and did not differ from that recorded in sham animals (p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 4D-E.

claim: SCI in neonates enhanced a calpain-mediated cleavage of Nav channels, as pointed out by the increased density of a ~ 120 kDa band on membrane fraction of Western blots probed by a pan-Nav antibody.
source: Consistent with these results, SCI in neonates enhanced a calpain-mediated cleavage of Nav channels, as pointed out by the increased density of a ~ 120 kDa band on membrane fraction of Western blots probed by a pan-Nav antibody (Figure 4F, left lane).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The acute bath application of MDL28170 reduced the ~120 kDa fragment.
source: Interestingly, the acute bath application of MDL28170 reduced the ~120 kDa fragment (p<0.05; Figure 4F, right lane) without affecting the prominent ~250 kDa representing the full-length form of Nav channels (p>0.05; Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4F.

claim: The MDL28170-induced decrease of the ~120 kDa fragment observed on membrane fraction was associated with a decrease in the density of immunostaining for Nav1.6.
source: Consistent with, the MDL28170-induced decrease of the ~120 kDa fragment observed on membrane fraction was associated with a decrease in the density of immunostaining for Nav1.6, the main α-subunits expressed at the axon initial segment of lumbar motoneurons (p<0.001; Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4G.

claim: MDL28170 reduced by 16% the amplitude of INaP.
source: MDL28170 reduced by 16% the amplitude of INaP (p<0.05; Figure 4H) without affecting its voltage activation threshold (p>0.05; Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings presented in Figure 4H.

claim: MDL28170 did not affect the voltage activation threshold of INaP.
source: MDL28170 reduced by 16% the amplitude of INaP (p<0.05; Figure 4H) without affecting its voltage activation threshold (p>0.05; Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings presented in Figure 4H.

claim: MDL28170 did not change INaP recorded from motoneurons in sham-operated controls.
source: In contrast, MDL28170 did not change INaP recorded from motoneurons in sham-operated controls (p<0.05; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This claim is supported by voltage-clamp recordings presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Bath-applied MDL 28170 increased by 21% the expression of KCC2 in its oligomeric ~240 kDa form.
source: Bath-applied MDL 28170 increased by 21% the expression of KCC2 in its oligomeric ~240 kDa form (p<0.05; Figure 4I) without affecting the monomeric ~140 kDa form (p>0.05; Figure 4I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4I.

claim: The addition of calpain-I in spinal cord homogenates from intact neonatal rat, dose-dependently reduced the expression of KCC2.
source: Furthermore, the addition of calpain-I in spinal cord homogenates from intact neonatal rat, dose-dependently reduced the expression of KCC2 (p<0.01; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: MDL 28170 increased KCC2 staining in the lateral ventral horn where motoneurons are located.
source: MDL 28170 increased KCC2 staining in the lateral ventral horn where motoneurons are located (p<0.05; Figure 4J).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 4J.

claim: Acute bath application of MDL28170 hyperpolarized motoneuronal EIPSP.
source: Acute bath application of MDL28170 hyperpolarized motoneuronal EIPSP (p<0.05, Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings presented in Figure 4K.

claim: The driving force on chloride (EIPSP-Vrest) was significantly more negative after MDL28170 treatment.
source: Because MDL28170 had no effect on the resting membrane potential (Vrest), the driving force on chloride (EIPSP-Vrest) was significantly more negative (p<0.05, Figure 4K).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings presented in Figure 4K.

claim: MDL28170 had no effect on EIPSP of motoneurons recorded from sham-operated animals.
source: MDL28170 had no effect on EIPSP of motoneurons recorded from sham-operated animals (p<0.05; Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by intracellular recordings presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: Bath-applied riluzole (5 µM) normalized the excitability of the SCI spinal cord.
source: Bath-applied riluzole (5 µM) normalized the excitability of the SCI spinal cord. The SLR was decreased and the LLR was abolished without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p<0.05, p<0.01 and p>0.05, respectively; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Riluzole decreased the SLR.
source: Bath-applied riluzole (5 µM) normalized the excitability of the SCI spinal cord. The SLR was decreased and the LLR was abolished without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p<0.05, p<0.01 and p>0.05, respectively; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Riluzole abolished the LLR.
source: Bath-applied riluzole (5 µM) normalized the excitability of the SCI spinal cord. The SLR was decreased and the LLR was abolished without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p<0.05, p<0.01 and p>0.05, respectively; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Riluzole did not affect the monosynaptic reflex.
source: Bath-applied riluzole (5 µM) normalized the excitability of the SCI spinal cord. The SLR was decreased and the LLR was abolished without affecting the monosynaptic reflex (p<0.05, p<0.01 and p>0.05, respectively; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Riluzole markedly reduced spontaneous bursting activity.
source: In addition, spontaneous bursting activity was markedly reduced (p<0.01; Figure 5D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5D-E.

claim: 4,9-ah-TTX reduced dorsal root-evoked motor outputs.
source: Similar results were obtained for dorsal root-evoked (p<0.05; Figure 5F–H) or spontaneous bursting (p<0.001; Figure 5I–J) motor outputs when the Nav1.6-mediated current was specifically blocked by 4,9-anhydro-tetrodotoxin (200 nM; 4,9-ah-TTX (Rosker et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5F-H.

claim: 4,9-ah-TTX reduced spontaneous bursting motor outputs.
source: Similar results were obtained for dorsal root-evoked (p<0.05; Figure 5F–H) or spontaneous bursting (p<0.001; Figure 5I–J) motor outputs when the Nav1.6-mediated current was specifically blocked by 4,9-anhydro-tetrodotoxin (200 nM; 4,9-ah-TTX (Rosker et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5I-J.

claim: The selective pharmacological enhancement of INaP with 100 nM of the steroidal alkaloid veratridine triggered LLR.
source: Conversely, the selective pharmacological enhancement of INaP with 100 nM of the steroidal alkaloid veratridine (Alkadhi and Tian, 1996; Tazerart et al., 2008) triggered LLR (p<0.01; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) and increased spontaneous bursting activity (p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Veratridine increased spontaneous bursting activity.
source: Conversely, the selective pharmacological enhancement of INaP with 100 nM of the steroidal alkaloid veratridine (Alkadhi and Tian, 1996; Tazerart et al., 2008) triggered LLR (p<0.01; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C) and increased spontaneous bursting activity (p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: The veratridine-induced motor responses were occluded by riluzole.
source: The veratridine-induced motor responses were occluded by riluzole (5 µM, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Blockade of ICaP by the L-type Ca2+ channel blocker nifedipine (20 µM) did not reduce either hyperreflexia or spontaneous bursting activity.
source: Blockade of the second persistent inward current 'ICaP' by the L-type Ca2+ channel blocker nifedipine (20 µM) did not reduce either hyperreflexia or spontaneous bursting activity (p>0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: The L-type Ca2+ channel enhancer Bay-K (10 µM) triggered LLR and spontaneous bursting activity in isolated spinal cord from control intact neonatal rats.
source: However, the L-type Ca2+ channel enhancer Bay-K (10 µM) triggered LLR and spontaneous bursting activity in isolated spinal cord from control intact neonatal rats (p<0.05; Figure 5—figure supplement 2F–J).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2F-J.

claim: PCPz used at 10 µM reduced the LLR.
source: PCPz used at the minimal concentration (10 µM) to restore KCC2 function after SCI (Liabeuf et al., 2017), reduced the LLR and spontaneous bursting activity in amplitude and frequency (p<0.01, p<0.01 and p<0.05 respectively; Figure 5K–O) with no effects on SLR or monosynaptic reflex amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5K-O.

claim: PCPz reduced spontaneous bursting activity in amplitude and frequency.
source: PCPz used at the minimal concentration (10 µM) to restore KCC2 function after SCI (Liabeuf et al., 2017), reduced the LLR and spontaneous bursting activity in amplitude and frequency (p<0.01, p<0.01 and p<0.05 respectively; Figure 5K–O) with no effects on SLR or monosynaptic reflex amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5K-O.

claim: PCPz had no effects on SLR or monosynaptic reflex amplitude.
source: PCPz used at the minimal concentration (10 µM) to restore KCC2 function after SCI (Liabeuf et al., 2017), reduced the LLR and spontaneous bursting activity in amplitude and frequency (p<0.01, p<0.01 and p<0.05 respectively; Figure 5K–O) with no effects on SLR or monosynaptic reflex amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 5K-O.

claim: When veratridine and DIOA were co-applied, enhanced LLR and spontaneous bursts were triggered.
source: At these concentrations, neither veratridine nor DIOA alone triggered either hyperreflexia or an increase in spontaneous bursts (gray, p>0.05; Figure 6A–F). However, when veratridine and DIOA were co-applied, enhanced LLR and spontaneous bursts were triggered (red, Figure 6A–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6A-H.

claim: Neither veratridine nor DIOA alone triggered either hyperreflexia or an increase in spontaneous bursts at the concentrations used.
source: At these concentrations, neither veratridine nor DIOA alone triggered either hyperreflexia or an increase in spontaneous bursts (gray, p>0.05; Figure 6A–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 6A-F.

claim: The main spasticity symptoms develop within one week following SCI in neonatal rats.
source: The main spasticity symptoms develop within one week following SCI in neonatal rats, and correlate with an early appearance of hyperexcitability in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the Results section.

claim: The emergence of spasticity is surprisingly faster in neonatal rats than in adult animals.
source: The emergence of spasticity is surprisingly faster than that of adult animals, which appears several weeks after the injury.
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on the data from this study and prior literature.

claim: A more active calpain-mediated proteolysis during early development may explain the age-dependent discrepancy in spasticity emergence.
source: A more active calpain-mediated proteolysis during early development may explain this age-dependent discrepancy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed age-dependent differences.

claim: Calpain proteolysis is necessary for the pruning of axons during development.
source: Indeed, calpain proteolysis is necessary for the pruning of axons during development (Yang et al., 2013) and the natural calpain inhibitory peptide, calpastatin, increases slowly in the CNS during the first weeks of life (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The natural calpain inhibitory peptide, calpastatin, increases slowly in the CNS during the first weeks of life.
source: Indeed, calpain proteolysis is necessary for the pruning of axons during development (Yang et al., 2013) and the natural calpain inhibitory peptide, calpastatin, increases slowly in the CNS during the first weeks of life (Li et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The lower presence of calpastatin in newborn rats may explain why hyperexcitability after a neonatal SCI developed faster.
source: The lower presence of this inhibitor in newborn rats may explain why hyperexcitability after a neonatal SCI developed faster.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the developmental expression of calpastatin.

claim: At birth, rat motoneurons overexpress NMDA receptors.
source: Also at birth, rat motoneurons overexpress NMDA receptors (Vinay et al., 2000) which have been demonstrated to be efficient in activating calpains in pathological conditions (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NMDA receptors have been demonstrated to be efficient in activating calpains in pathological conditions.
source: Also at birth, rat motoneurons overexpress NMDA receptors (Vinay et al., 2000) which have been demonstrated to be efficient in activating calpains in pathological conditions (Zhou et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The low expression of calpastatin combined with a high expression of NMDA receptors may contribute to a fast increase of motoneuronal excitability after a SCI in newborn rats.
source: In sum, the low expression of calpastatin combined with a high expression of NMDA receptors may contribute to a fast increase of motoneuronal excitability after a SCI in newborn rats.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the combined effects of calpastatin and NMDA receptors.

claim: Hyperexcitability emerges in vitro in the form of high-frequency spontaneous bursting activity and enhanced, prolonged sensory-evoked LLR.
source: This hyperexcitability emerges in vitro in the form of high-frequency spontaneous bursting activity and enhanced, prolonged sensory-evoked LLR.
evidence: This is a summary of the in vitro findings presented in Figure 3.

claim: Both high-frequency spontaneous bursting activity and enhanced, prolonged sensory-evoked LLR are dependent on INaP and KCC2 dysfunction.
source: We provided evidence that both are dependent on INaP and KCC2 dysfunction.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the pharmacological experiments presented in Figures 4-6.

claim: INaP plays an important role in the operation of the spinal locomotor network.
source: INaP plays an important role in the operation of the spinal locomotor network (Tazerart et al., 2007; Tazerart et al., 2008; Brocard et al., 2010; Bouhadfane et al., 2013; Brocard et al., 2013) and its increase after SCI promotes prolonged plateau potential firing in motoneurons and hyperreflexia, both in animal models and humans (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Kitzman, 2009; Theiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The increase of INaP after SCI promotes prolonged plateau potential firing in motoneurons and hyperreflexia, both in animal models and humans.
source: INaP plays an important role in the operation of the spinal locomotor network (Tazerart et al., 2007; Tazerart et al., 2008; Brocard et al., 2010; Bouhadfane et al., 2013; Brocard et al., 2013) and its increase after SCI promotes prolonged plateau potential firing in motoneurons and hyperreflexia, both in animal models and humans (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Kitzman, 2009; Theiss et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Supersensitivity of motoneurons to residual serotonin after SCI leads to the facilitation of INaP.
source: Supersensitivity of motoneurons to residual serotonin after SCI leads to the facilitation of INaP (Harvey et al., 2006a; Harvey et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calpain-dependent cleavage of Nav channels upregulates INaP in lumbar motoneurons.
source: Here, we demonstrate that calpain-dependent cleavage of Nav channels also upregulates INaP in lumbar motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Proteolyzed Nav channels remain in the plasma membrane and might interfere with biophysical properties of full-length voltage-gated channels.
source: As previously observed after a traumatic brain injury (von Reyn et al., 2009), proteolyzed Nav channels remain in the plasma membrane and thus might interfere with biophysical properties of full-length voltage-gated channels (Michailidis et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and involves speculative reasoning.

claim: Some determinants governing the inactivation of Nav channels are sensitive to proteases, which can increase INaP.
source: On the other hand, some determinants governing the inactivation of Nav channels are sensitive to proteases, which can increase INaP (Armstrong et al., 1973; Gonoi and Hille, 1987; Clarkson, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calpain-mediated cleavage of Nav1.6 channels in HEK-293 cells up-regulates INaP.
source: Whatever the mechanisms, a clear relationship is given by our previous study in which calpain-mediated cleavage of Nav1.6 channels in HEK-293 cells up-regulates INaP (Brocard et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nav1.6 channels are highly expressed in spinal motoneurons.
source: Because Nav1.6 channels are highly expressed in spinal motoneurons (Alessandri-Haber et al., 2002; Duflocq et al., 2008; Brocard et al., 2016), their cleavage likely contributes to increase INaP after SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cleavage of Nav1.6 channels likely contributes to increase INaP after SCI.
source: Because Nav1.6 channels are highly expressed in spinal motoneurons (Alessandri-Haber et al., 2002; Duflocq et al., 2008; Brocard et al., 2016), their cleavage likely contributes to increase INaP after SCI.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression of Nav1.6 channels and their cleavage.

claim: Pharmacological inhibition of Nav1.6 channels significantly reduced hyperexcitability after SCI.
source: This is consistent with our result that pharmacological inhibition of Nav1.6 channels significantly reduced hyperexcitability after SCI.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Mutation of Nav1.6 channels leads to severe myoclonic spasms with a fivefold increase of INaP.
source: Further support comes from mutation of Nav1.6 channels that leads to severe myoclonic spasms with a fivefold increase of INaP (Veeramah et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The rescue of INaP by MDL28170 is only partial.
source: It is noteworthy that the rescue of INaP by MDL28170 is only partial.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: Calpain-independent mechanism(s) may contribute to increase INaP.
source: Although an incomplete block of calpains by MDL28170 cannot be excluded, calpain-independent mechanism(s) may contribute to increase INaP.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the partial rescue of INaP.

claim: The activation of 5HT2 receptors facilitates INaP.
source: Since the activation of 5HT2 receptors facilitates INaP (Harvey et al., 2006b), the constitutive activation of 5HT2 receptors after SCI (Murray et al., 2010) might be one of them.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The constitutive activation of 5HT2 receptors after SCI might contribute to increase INaP.
source: Since the activation of 5HT2 receptors facilitates INaP (Harvey et al., 2006b), the constitutive activation of 5HT2 receptors after SCI (Murray et al., 2010) might be one of them.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: The amount of full-length Nav channels (~250 kDa) at the plasma membrane never changed after either the post-SCI activation of calpains or their inhibition by a MDL28170 treatment.
source: Also, the amount of full-length Nav channels (~250 kDa) at the plasma membrane never changed after either the post-SCI activation of calpains (Brocard et al., 2016) or their inhibition by a MDL28170 treatment (see Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 4F and cited literature.

claim: It is possible that the translocation of fragments into the nucleus maintains constant the expression level of the full-length channel at the membrane by regulating the Nav channel transcription.
source: As a compensation mechanism depending on the number of proteolytic fragments, it is possible that the translocation of fragments into the nucleus maintains constant the expression level of the full-length channel at the membrane by regulating the Nav channel transcription (Onwuli et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: Synaptic disinhibition of motoneurons after SCI contributes to spasticity and results from a decreased expression of KCC2.
source: Synaptic disinhibition of motoneurons after SCI also contributes to spasticity and results from a decreased expression of KCC2 (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A down-regulation of KCC2 has been described after SCI.
source: Although a down-regulation of KCC2 has been described after SCI (Boulenguez et al., 2010; Côté et al., 2014; Mòdol et al., 2014; Chang et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2018), the causal molecular mechanisms remain unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of calpains is one of the molecular basis for disinhibition of motoneurons after SCI.
source: Here, we provide evidence that activation of calpains is one of the molecular basis for disinhibition of motoneurons after SCI.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Exogenous application of active calpains reduces KCC2 in its oligo and monomeric forms in spinal cord homogenates.
source: A direct relationship between calpain and KCC2 is given by our studies on spinal cord homogenates, in which exogenous application of active calpains reduces KCC2 in its oligo and monomeric forms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: KCC2 has two predicted sites (PEST motifs) for cleavage by calpain within the C-terminal domain.
source: The sensitivity of KCC2 to calpain is consistent with the presence of two predicted sites (PEST motifs) for cleavage by calpain within the C-terminal domain (Mercado et al., 2006; Acton et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ability of KCC2 to extrude Cl- requires the C-terminal domain.
source: Since the ability of KCC2 to extrude Cl- requires the C-terminal domain (Mercado et al., 2006; Acton et al., 2012) and that the KCC2 antibody targets the C-tail, its cleavage by calpains after SCI likely accounts for both the immunostaining decrease of KCC2 at the plasma membrane and the loss of chloride extrusion resulting in the depolarizing shift of EIPSP in motoneurons (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function relationship of KCC2 and prior literature.

claim: The cleavage of KCC2 by calpains after SCI likely accounts for the immunostaining decrease of KCC2 at the plasma membrane.
source: Since the ability of KCC2 to extrude Cl- requires the C-terminal domain (Mercado et al., 2006; Acton et al., 2012) and that the KCC2 antibody targets the C-tail, its cleavage by calpains after SCI likely accounts for both the immunostaining decrease of KCC2 at the plasma membrane and the loss of chloride extrusion resulting in the depolarizing shift of EIPSP in motoneurons (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function relationship of KCC2 and prior literature.

claim: The cleavage of KCC2 by calpains after SCI likely accounts for the loss of chloride extrusion resulting in the depolarizing shift of EIPSP in motoneurons.
source: Since the ability of KCC2 to extrude Cl- requires the C-terminal domain (Mercado et al., 2006; Acton et al., 2012) and that the KCC2 antibody targets the C-tail, its cleavage by calpains after SCI likely accounts for both the immunostaining decrease of KCC2 at the plasma membrane and the loss of chloride extrusion resulting in the depolarizing shift of EIPSP in motoneurons (Boulenguez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure-function relationship of KCC2 and prior literature.

claim: An acute inhibition of calpains by MDL28170 rapidly restores both EIPSP and KCC2.
source: The tight relationship between the calpain-mediated proteolysis of KCC2 and the altered Cl- homeostasis is supported by our observation that an acute inhibition of calpains by MDL28170 rapidly restores both EIPSP and KCC2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The rapid rescue of KCC2 by the acute application of MDL28170 is in agreement with the fast pharmacodynamic of MDL28170 to cross the brain blood barrier.
source: The rapid rescue of KCC2 by the acute application of MDL28170 is in agreement with the fast pharmacodynamic of MDL28170 to cross the brain blood barrier (Markgraf et al., 1998) and the extremely high rate (minutes) in KCC2 turnover at the plasma membrane (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: KCC2 has an extremely high rate (minutes) in turnover at the plasma membrane.
source: The rapid rescue of KCC2 by the acute application of MDL28170 is in agreement with the fast pharmacodynamic of MDL28170 to cross the brain blood barrier (Markgraf et al., 1998) and the extremely high rate (minutes) in KCC2 turnover at the plasma membrane (Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Oligomers of KCC2 appear more sensitive to calpains than monomers after SCI.
source: Regarding the rescue of KCC2 by MDL28170, oligomers appear more sensitive to calpains than monomers after SCI.
evidence: This is an observation based on the experimental data presented in Figure 4I.

claim: Phosphorylation regulates the vulnerability of substrates to calpains.
source: As phosphorylation regulates the vulnerability of substrates to calpains (Sprague et al., 2008), the post-SCI dephosphorylation of KCC2 at the serine 960 (Mòdol et al., 2014), in the vicinity of PEST motifs, might contribute to sensitize more oligomers to calpains.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The post-SCI dephosphorylation of KCC2 at the serine 960 might contribute to sensitize more oligomers to calpains.
source: As phosphorylation regulates the vulnerability of substrates to calpains (Sprague et al., 2008), the post-SCI dephosphorylation of KCC2 at the serine 960 (Mòdol et al., 2014), in the vicinity of PEST motifs, might contribute to sensitize more oligomers to calpains.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: KCC2 and INaP appear to cooperate in promoting spinal hyperexcitability after SCI.
source: Our results suggest that KCC2 and INaP appear to cooperate in promoting spinal hyperexcitability after SCI.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: A modeling investigation demonstrated that the depolarizing shift of EIPSP after SCI facilitates the recruitment of persistent inward currents in motoneurons.
source: In line with this, a modeling investigation demonstrated that the depolarizing shift of EIPSP after SCI facilitates the recruitment of persistent inward currents in motoneurons (Venugopal et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The depolarizing shift of EIPSP after a decrease in KCC2 may enable the unusual long-lasting depolarization reported in motoneurons after SCI.
source: The depolarizing shift of EIPSP after a decrease in KCC2 may enable the unusual long-lasting depolarization reported in motoneurons after SCI (Li et al., 2004), which is required to recruit INaP.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: INaP will promote plateau potentials resulting in self-sustaining spiking in motoneurons.
source: In turn, INaP will promote plateau potentials resulting in self-sustaining spiking in motoneurons (Li and Bennett, 2003; Bouhadfane et al., 2013) that drives spasticity (Bennett et al., 2001; Gorassini, 2004; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Self-sustaining spiking in motoneurons drives spasticity.
source: In turn, INaP will promote plateau potentials resulting in self-sustaining spiking in motoneurons (Li and Bennett, 2003; Bouhadfane et al., 2013) that drives spasticity (Bennett et al., 2001; Gorassini, 2004; Li et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Termination of plateau potentials by hyperpolarizing the motoneuron will be much more difficult in a context of disinhibition.
source: Furthermore, termination of plateau potentials by hyperpolarizing the motoneuron (Hounsgaard et al., 1984) will be much more difficult in a context of disinhibition; this may explain the fasciculation-like contractions commonly recorded in spastic subjects (Gorassini, 2004; Winslow et al., 2009; Zijdewind and Thomas, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: INaP-blockers such as riluzole likely alleviate spasticity by decoupling the tandem response driven by enhanced INaP and decreased KCC2.
source: Therefore, INaP-blockers such as riluzole, or KCC2 enhancers likely alleviate spasticity (Brocard et al., 2016; Liabeuf et al., 2017) by decoupling the tandem response driven by enhanced INaP and decreased KCC2.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature and the current study.

claim: KCC2 enhancers likely alleviate spasticity by decoupling the tandem response driven by enhanced INaP and decreased KCC2.
source: Therefore, INaP-blockers such as riluzole, or KCC2 enhancers likely alleviate spasticity (Brocard et al., 2016; Liabeuf et al., 2017) by decoupling the tandem response driven by enhanced INaP and decreased KCC2.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature and the current study.

claim: Riluzole is currently approved for humans affected by Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).
source: The riluzole is currently approved for humans affected by Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge.

claim: Clinical trials are currently in progress to test the neuroprotective effects of riluzole in the acute phase of SCI.
source: Our data provide strong preclinical evidence for translation to chronic SCI subjects, a process that will likely be facilitated by clinical trials that are currently in progress to test the neuroprotective effects of riluzole in the acute phase of SCI (Grossman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Calpains exist in the CNS mainly as two major isoforms, µ-calpain (calpain-I) and m-calpain (calpain-II) that differ on the range of [Ca2+] required for their activation (µM and mM, respectively).
source: Calpains exist in the CNS mainly as two major isoforms, µ-calpain (calpain-I) and m-calpain (calpain-II) that differ on the range of [Ca2+] required for their activation (µM and mM, respectively).
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: The expression of calpain-I increases after SCI in neonatal rats.
source: As previously observed in adult rodents (Springer et al., 1997; Du et al., 1999; Schumacher et al., 1999; Yu et al., 2013), we found that the expression of calpain-I increases after SCI in neonatal rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 2 and citations to prior literature.

claim: The protease protein expression does not necessarily correspond to enzyme's catalytic activity.
source: However, the protease protein expression does not necessarily correspond to enzyme's catalytic activity.
evidence: This is a statement of general scientific knowledge.

claim: After a traumatic brain injury (TBI), calpain-I and -II appear neuroprotective and neurodegenerative, respectively.
source: After a traumatic brain injury (TBI), calpain-I and -II appear neuroprotective and neurodegenerative, respectively (Baudry and Bi, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The respective contribution of calpain-I and -II in the hyperexcitability of motoneurons after SCI remains to be clarified.
source: Therefore, the respective contribution of calpain-I and -II in the hyperexcitability of motoneurons after SCI remains to be clarified.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation or future direction for research.

claim: Calpain-mediated changes in motoneurons alone are unlikely to account for all the post-injury spinal hyperexcitability.
source: Calpain-mediated changes in motoneurons alone are unlikely to account for all the post-injury spinal hyperexcitability.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging the complexity of spinal hyperexcitability.

claim: Premotor excitatory interneurons, including locomotor network-related interneurons, may play a critical role in initiating muscle spasm activity.
source: Premotor excitatory interneurons, including locomotor network-related interneurons, may play a critical role in initiating muscle spasm activity (Husch et al., 2012; Bellardita et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most sensory-evoked LLRs are composed of a fictive locomotor episode.
source: In line with this, we found that most sensory-evoked LLRs are composed of a fictive locomotor episode, suggesting enhanced sensory recruitment of the locomotor central pattern generator (CPG).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Part of muscle spasm, and especially clonus (involuntary rhythmic contractions), might be a manifestation of a hyperexcitable locomotor CPG.
source: This leads us to believe that part of muscle spasm, and especially clonus (involuntary rhythmic contractions), might be a manifestation of a hyperexcitable locomotor CPG.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the experimental data.

claim: Enhanced sensory-evoked LLR has been previously described in the sacrocaudal spinal cord from adult SCI rodents.
source: Enhanced sensory-evoked LLR has been previously described in the sacrocaudal spinal cord from adult SCI rodents but differs in some aspects from our results with neonatal lumbar motoneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ICaP contributes to sacrocaudal hyperreflexia by promoting plateaus in motoneurons.
source: Indeed, ICaP contributes to sacrocaudal hyperreflexia by promoting plateaus in motoneurons (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004) while disinhibition appears negligible (Bellardita et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Disinhibition appears negligible in sacrocaudal hyperreflexia.
source: Indeed, ICaP contributes to sacrocaudal hyperreflexia by promoting plateaus in motoneurons (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004) while disinhibition appears negligible (Bellardita et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The ICaP appears to have a negligible role in lumbar hyperreflexia from neonatal SCI rats.
source: The ICaP appears to have a negligible role in lumbar hyperreflexia from neonatal SCI rats, in line with previous work showing a full maturation of L-type Ca2+ channels at second/third post-natal weeks (Jiang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and citations to prior literature.

claim: L-type Ca2+ channels fully mature at second/third post-natal weeks.
source: The ICaP appears to have a negligible role in lumbar hyperreflexia from neonatal SCI rats, in line with previous work showing a full maturation of L-type Ca2+ channels at second/third post-natal weeks (Jiang et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some L-type Ca2+ channels are already expressed in the first post-natal week.
source: However, we also demonstrate that some of these channels are already expressed in the first post-natal week, as their pharmacological activation by Bay-K triggered LLRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: It is likely that the contribution of L-type Ca2+ channels to the LLR increases with age.
source: Thus, it is likely that the contribution of L-type Ca2+ channels to the LLR increases with age.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the developmental expression of L-type Ca2+ channels.

claim: Temperature and ionic composition of the extracellular medium may account for the relative contribution of INaP and ICaP in generating LLRs.
source: Alternatively, temperature and ionic composition of the extracellular medium may account for the relative contribution of INaP and ICaP in generating LLRs.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differences observed between studies.

claim: In vitro studies in adults were performed at room temperature with high extracellular [Ca2+] (≥2.5 mM).
source: In vitro studies in adults were performed at room temperature with high extracellular [Ca2+] (≥2.5 mM) (Li and Bennett, 2003; Li et al., 2004; Bellardita et al., 2017), far from physiological conditions [body temperature 37°C; 1.2 mM of Ca2+ in the CSF (Nicholson et al., 1977; Jones and Keep, 1988; Brocard et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Ca2+ currents are potentiated at room temperature with high extracellular [Ca2+].
source: As a consequence, Ca2+ currents are potentiated (Carlin et al., 2000; Carlin et al., 2009), INaP is reduced (Tazerart et al., 2008) and thermosensitive INaP-dependent plateaus in motoneurons are dampened down (Bouhadfane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: INaP is reduced at room temperature with high extracellular [Ca2+].
source: As a consequence, Ca2+ currents are potentiated (Carlin et al., 2000; Carlin et al., 2009), INaP is reduced (Tazerart et al., 2008) and thermosensitive INaP-dependent plateaus in motoneurons are dampened down (Bouhadfane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Thermosensitive INaP-dependent plateaus in motoneurons are dampened down at room temperature with high extracellular [Ca2+].
source: As a consequence, Ca2+ currents are potentiated (Carlin et al., 2000; Carlin et al., 2009), INaP is reduced (Tazerart et al., 2008) and thermosensitive INaP-dependent plateaus in motoneurons are dampened down (Bouhadfane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The disinhibition seen in the SCI lumbar enlargement, linked to the decrease of KCC2, seems unimportant in the sacrocaudal spinal cord.
source: Also, the disinhibition seen in the SCI lumbar enlargement, linked to the decrease of KCC2 (Boulenguez et al., 2010), seems unimportant in the sacrocaudal spinal cord (Bellardita et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Diversity of KCC2 expression between motoneurons innervating distinct muscles may account for the discrepancy in disinhibition between lumbar and sacrocaudal spinal cord.
source: Diversity of KCC2 expression between motoneurons innervating distinct muscles (Ueno et al., 2002) or variation in the sacral inhibitory circuitry (Jankowska et al., 1978) may account for this discrepancy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: Variation in the sacral inhibitory circuitry may account for the discrepancy in disinhibition between lumbar and sacrocaudal spinal cord.
source: Diversity of KCC2 expression between motoneurons innervating distinct muscles (Ueno et al., 2002) or variation in the sacral inhibitory circuitry (Jankowska et al., 1978) may account for this discrepancy.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on prior literature.

claim: Spinal cord level-specific differences in neuronal responses to SCI are probable with respect to the special anatomy and function of the sacrocaudal spinal cord.
source: Spinal cord level-specific differences in neuronal responses to SCI are probable with respect to the special anatomy and function of the sacrocaudal spinal cord (Ritz et al., 1992; Ritz et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on prior literature.

claim: The discovery of calpain as a new upstream mechanism leading to spasticity is of special importance given the lack of translational results obtained from previously tested therapeutic approaches.
source: To conclude, our study sheds light on the etiology of spasticity and opens novel perspectives to develop therapies by targeting calpains. The discovery of calpain as a new upstream mechanism leading to spasticity, is of special importance given the lack of translational results obtained from previously tested therapeutic approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of the findings.

claim: Spinal maladaptive mechanisms triggered by calpain start taking place within the first hours after injury in the SCI model.
source: Since spinal maladaptive mechanisms triggered by calpain start taking place within the first hours after injury in our SCI model, it is conceivable that early therapies against calpain might show a higher effectiveness.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing early changes after SCI.

claim: Early therapies against calpain might show a higher effectiveness.
source: Since spinal maladaptive mechanisms triggered by calpain start taking place within the first hours after injury in our SCI model, it is conceivable that early therapies against calpain might show a higher effectiveness.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic implications.

claim: Altered chloride homeostasis and proteolysis of Nav channels have been implicated in traumatic brain injury for which calpains are recruited.
source: Because altered chloride homeostasis and proteolysis of Nav channels have been implicated in other neurological disorders such as traumatic brain injury for which calpains are recruited (Kahle et al., 2008; von Reyn et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018), the involvement of calpains might be broadened to other pathologies leading to an excitatory/inhibitory imbalance.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The involvement of calpains might be broadened to other pathologies leading to an excitatory/inhibitory imbalance.
source: Because altered chloride homeostasis and proteolysis of Nav channels have been implicated in other neurological disorders such as traumatic brain injury for which calpains are recruited (Kahle et al., 2008; von Reyn et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2018), the involvement of calpains might be broadened to other pathologies leading to an excitatory/inhibitory imbalance.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the broader implications of the findings.

claim: The acute i.p. administration of MDL28170 at 60 mg/kg or 120 mg/kg dose-dependently reduced the number of spontaneous muscle twitches.
source: The acute intraperitoneal injection (i.p.) of MDL28170 at minimal or maximal effective doses for the reduction of calpain activity in the CNS (Kawamura et al., 2005; Thompson et al., 2010), dose-dependently reduced the number of spontaneous muscle twitches (p<0.001; Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: At the highest dose (120 mg/kg), twitches were less frequent up to 9 hr compared to vehicle-treated animals.
source: At the highest dose (120 mg/kg), twitches were less frequent up to 9 hr compared to vehicle-treated animals and temporarily dropped to levels similar to those found in intact animals over a period from 2 to 5 hr post-injection (Figure 1G, dashed line).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: MDL28170 used at 120 mg/kg did not reduce spontaneous twitches in sham-operated animals.
source: Note that MDL28170 used at 120 mg/kg did not reduce spontaneous twitches in sham-operated animals suggesting that the effect of the drug was specific to rats with SCI and did not result from lethargy (p>0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The acute inhibition of calpains with MDL28170 decreased the duration of EMG responses to tail-pinch in SCI neonatal rats.
source: In addition to spasms reduction, the acute inhibition of calpains with MDL28170 decreased the duration of EMG responses to tail-pinch in SCI neonatal rats (p<0.05, Figure 1H) without affecting the threshold to mechanical stimuli (p>0.05, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: MDL28170 did not affect the threshold to mechanical stimuli in SCI neonatal rats.
source: In addition to spasms reduction, the acute inhibition of calpains with MDL28170 decreased the duration of EMG responses to tail-pinch in SCI neonatal rats (p<0.05, Figure 1H) without affecting the threshold to mechanical stimuli (p>0.05, Figure 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by EMG data presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Data revealed a causal relationship between the activation of calpain and the development of spasticity in the neonatal SCI model.
source: In sum, data revealed a causal relationship between the activation of calpain and the development of spasticity in the neonatal SCI model.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Expression of calpain-II did not change after SCI.
source: Expression of calpain-II did not change after SCI (p>0.05; Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data presented in Figure 2.

claim: The SLR did not change regardless of age in sham-operated animals.
source: The SLR (the early transient 40 ms response) did not change regardless of age (p>0.05, in black, Figure 3D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3D-G.

claim: The SLR gradually increased after SCI.
source: By contrast, the SLR gradually increased after SCI (p<0.001, in red, Figure 3D–G) and a long-lasting reflex (LLR, red traces; Figure 3A–C), almost absent in sham-operated rats, was noticeable 24 hr post-surgery.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3D-G.

claim: A long-lasting reflex (LLR) was noticeable 24 hr post-surgery after SCI.
source: By contrast, the SLR gradually increased after SCI (p<0.001, in red, Figure 3D–G) and a long-lasting reflex (LLR, red traces; Figure 3A–C), almost absent in sham-operated rats, was noticeable 24 hr post-surgery.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3A-C.

claim: An interpulse interval of at least 4 min was required to avoid a use-dependent decline of the LLR.
source: Note that an interpulse interval of at least 4 min was required to avoid a use-dependent decline of the LLR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The LLR gradually increased after SCI and differed significantly from sham-operated rats as early as 2–3 d post-SCI.
source: The LLR gradually increased after SCI and differed significantly from sham-operated rats as early as 2–3 d post-SCI (p<0.001, Figure 3H), transforming the unimodal peristimulus time histograms (PSTHs) into a bimodal distribution (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3H.

claim: One week after SCI, the LLR lasted 9.0 ± 0.6 s.
source: One week after SCI, the LLR lasted 9.0 ± 0.6 s (n = 52 spinal cords, Figure 3C) and the stimulus threshold was markedly decreased (p<0.001, Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data presented in Figure 3C.

claim: The stimulus threshold was markedly decreased one week after SCI.
